description: Two-dimensional grid layouts, plus media queries that adapt to any screen.

screens.body:
Grid lays items out in rows AND columns at once — a real two-dimensional layout. Flexbox handles a line; grid handles the whole page section.

Turn it on with display: grid on the parent, then describe your columns with grid-template-columns.

Think of it as drawing the table first, then dropping content into the cells.

options: Rows and columns at the same time
check.question: What can grid lay out?

screens.heading: Grid is a table you design

screens.body:
grid-template-columns describes each column's width. The star of the show is fr — a "fraction" of the available space.

1fr 1fr 1fr makes three equal columns. 2fr 1fr makes the first twice as wide as the second — like flex ratios, but for columns.

You can mix units: 200px 1fr gives a fixed sidebar plus a flexible main area.
screens.heading: Defining columns with fr
screens.keyPoint: fr = a fraction of free space. Mix with px.

screens.body:
gap sets the gutters between grid cells — one property for both row and column gaps.

Items can span multiple cells: grid-column: span 2 makes an item two columns wide. Great for featured cards in a gallery.

Explicit placement (grid-column: 1 / 3) exists too, but span covers most real layouts.

check.question: How do you make a grid item two columns wide?

screens.heading: Gaps and spanning
screens.keyPoint: gap = gutters. span N = stretch across N cells.

screens.body:
Responsive design means your layout adapts to the screen — one column on a phone, three on a desktop.

The standard approach is mobile-first: design for the small screen first, then add rules for bigger screens.

Small screens are the constraint that forces clarity. If it works on a phone, it works anywhere.

options: Adapts its layout to the screen size
check.question: What does responsive mean?

screens.heading: Responsive = adapt to screen
screens.keyPoint: Mobile-first: small screen first, enhance upward.

options: Only when the screen is 768px wide or wider
check.question: When does @media (min-width: 768px) apply?

screens.heading: Media queries: CSS with conditions

screens.body:
You don't need a query for every device — a few common breakpoints cover nearly everything.

768px is the classic tablet breakpoint, 1024px the classic desktop one. Design your layout to change at those widths.

Start with the phone layout as your base CSS, then layer on tablet and desktop upgrades with min-width queries.

check.question: Which breakpoints do developers commonly use?

screens.heading: Common breakpoints

screens.body:
Fixed pixel widths are the enemy of responsive pages — a 1200px-wide image blows out a 375px phone screen.

max-width: 100% on images keeps them inside their container: they shrink on small screens but never stretch past their natural size.

Same idea for text: avoid tiny fixed font sizes, and let line lengths stay readable by constraining container widths.

check.question: How do you keep images from overflowing phones?

screens.heading: Fluid images and text
screens.keyPoint: max-width: 100% keeps images inside their container.
